<<Sterling Shadows Over Luton>>

Section 1  
EasyJet ended the year with fuller aircraft and record passenger traffic, yet the balance sheet told a harsher story. Revenues pushed past £5bn as 80.2 million people flew with the airline, but fares were nudged downward to keep seats filled in a tough market. When the results landed, the headline was unavoidable: profits before tax slid from £494m to £408m, a 17% fall, and the slump in sterling after the Brexit vote added more than £100m in extra costs even as fuel was cheaper in dollar terms.

Section 2  
Inside headquarters near the airport control tower, executives framed the year as a test of strategy rather than nerve. Carolyn McCall argued that the airline’s push to secure first or second position at major European airports—paired with tighter cost discipline and better service—was a dare to outlast rivals amid bankruptcies and operational stumbles across the industry. Still, Brexit cast a long operational shadow: to keep flying freely within Europe after 2019, EasyJet signaled it would adjust rules so the company remains majority owned and controlled by EU nationals, leaning in part on the founder Stelios Haji-Ioannou’s UK-Cypriot status to meet the threshold.

Section 3  
The proposed shareholder measures—potentially forcing some UK investors to sell if needed—were described as technical, but they carried a deeper message about how markets and politics now steer corporate life in modern society. For customers, the change might feel distant, like watching fishing boats alter course because the tide shifted far offshore; for investors, it was a reminder that governance can turn quickly when borders and regulations are rewritten. Yet the market response offered a small treat: shares rose strongly on signs of high forward bookings and improved revenue early in the new financial year, helped by capacity leaving the market and giving the airline a clearer runway ahead.
